sources.interpretation: The primary guide distinguishes 20-second ECS monitoring from explicitly choosing ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilizationHighResolution or ECSServiceAverageMemoryUtilizationHighResolution. Updating monitoring requires deployment completion; console availability also requires tasks emitting at 20 seconds.

safety.network: Owned private VPC/subnet; no gateway, NAT, public IP, execution role or load balancer

polling.scope: Each monitoring transition is observed for 120 seconds without PutScalingPolicy. No tasks or metric publication; adaptation driven by real emission remains unobserved.

findings.claim: The standard ECS CPU and memory predefined metric types select 60-second alarms even when both ECS metrics are configured at 20 seconds, including after an explicit same-policy standard-metric rewrite.

Explicitly rewriting the same policies to ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilizationHighResolution and ECSServiceAverageMemoryUtilizationHighResolution succeeds with zero tasks and selects 20-second managed alarms. Monitoring was configured at 20 seconds; no actual metric emission was necessary for these observed API writes and alarm creation.

Monitoring updates alone did not change managed alarm names, action identity, metric selectors, thresholds, periods, evaluation counts or captured optional field presence in any of the three 120-second observation windows. The mixed CPU20/memory60 update retained both high-resolution policies and alarms; resetting monitoring to an empty configuration retained the previously selected CPU20/memory60 alarms.

Explicitly selecting the high-resolution CPU type and standard memory type after mixed monitoring selected CPU Period20/High3/Low30 and memory Period60/High3/Low15. Explicitly selecting both standard types after reset selected Period60/High3/Low15 for both metrics.

All eight explicit policy rewrites preserved each policy's PolicyARN, CreationTime and createdBy-suffixed AlarmActions identity, but replaced both managed alarm names, including the identical standard-metric rewrite.

All observed managed alarms used AWS/ECS, CPUUtilization or MemoryUtilization, ClusterName and ServiceName dimensions, Statistic Average, and Unit Percent. High used GreaterThanThreshold; Low used LessThanThreshold. DatapointsToAlarm, TreatMissingData and Metrics were absent from the native alarm responses.

Cleanup removed both policies, the scalable target, all observed managed alarms, the owned subnet and VPC. Final service and cluster observations were INACTIVE with zero task counts; running/stopped task lists and VPC network-interface list were empty. The task definition was deregistered and deletion accepted, but its final observed state was DELETE_IN_PROGRESS. Existing linked roles were not mutated or deleted.

uncertainties: No task was started and no metric was published. Actual-emission-dependent adaptation, live scaling response, and console gating after a real deployment are unobserved; the bounded no-change windows do not prove that alarms can never adapt later.

The primary faster-target-tracking guide describes monitoring and high-resolution predefined policy selection as separate steps. Its deployment/emission prerequisites must not be converted into a claim of automatic standard-to-high-resolution policy switching.
This capture does not test creating a HighResolution policy before monitoring has ever been configured at 20 seconds, or determine whether that unsupported ordering is rejected.
Task-definition deletion is asynchronous. DELETE_IN_PROGRESS is the final captured tombstone, not proof of completed physical deletion.

additionalPrimarySources.interpretation: Documents distinct HighResolution ECS CPU/memory predefined metric types for 20-second evaluation and says to enable high-resolution metrics in ECS before creating such policies.
